title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
claim: Conditioning a frozen pretrained generator directly on projected neural signals through a dedicated adapter enables end-to-end reconstruction without an intermediate stimulus representation.
layout: Single wide panel, looping left-to-right then right-to-left, with annotated module boxes
description: A single wide flow diagram that loops through a U-shape. At the bottom left, a cartoon brain wearing headphones represents the fMRI input, labeled brain data [B, 6 ROIs, voxels]. An arrow goes up to a top row of three pastel green-to-blue gradient boxes: RoiProjector, Brain-Token Generator, and fMRI Adapter for Audio. Small captions under each box give tensor shapes and the role of the module. From the adapter, a line labeled Empty Text drops down and branches into orange and blue connectors that feed a row of DiT Block cells at the bottom right. Noise latent Z_t on the right passes through the DiT to Z_t-1, then to a frozen VAE decoder trapezoid with a spectrogram-like purple bar icon. A dashed arrow leads back toward the brain, marked with evaluation metrics.
caption: General overview of our approach. fMRI responses from auditory ROIs are projected and transformed into brain tokens, which are injected into the cross-attention layers of a Diffusion Transformer via a dedicated adapter. The model is conditioned solely on brain activity (empty text prompt) and generates audio through a frozen latent diffusion backbone.
abstract: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation. MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.
